t: Minimum Sum of Mountain Triplets I
o: Find indices i < j < k with nums[i] < nums[j] and nums[k] < nums[j], minimizing the sum. With n <= 50 even checking all triples works, but the clean O(n) way uses running prefix minima and suffix minima: for each peak j, the best mountain using j as peak pairs it with the smallest element strictly left and strictly right smaller than nums[j].
k: For a fixed peak j, the optimal sides are the minimum element before j and the minimum element after j.
Prefix/suffix minimum arrays turn the cubic brute force into a linear scan.
A triplet exists at peak j only if both side minima are strictly less than nums[j].

a.i: Try every (i,j,k) and track the minimum valid sum. Fine for n <= 50.
s: If nums[i]<nums[j] and nums[k]<nums[j], update the answer.
a.t: O(n^3) — all triples checked; fine for n <= 50.

a.i: Precompute sufMin[j] = min(nums[j..n-1]) and scan left keeping preMin. Peak j contributes preMin-before + nums[j] + sufMin-after whenever both are strictly smaller than nums[j].
s: Scan j from left, maintaining the strict prefix minimum.
Update the answer when both neighbors qualify; return -1 if never.

w: In an interview, state the brute force, then upgrade to prefix/suffix minima. Strictness matters: equal values on either side disqualify a peak (example 3 has no valid triplet). Edge cases: monotonic arrays return -1. Follow-up: version II raises n, forcing the O(n) solution.
